title: Confidence intervals
examples: What does a 95 percent confidence interval actually mean?
How do I calculate the margin of error if I know the standard deviation?
What must be true about my data before I can use a confidence interval?

explain.say: Today we learn about confidence intervals for estimating population means. First, we need to understand the margin of error. The margin of error gives us a range around our sample mean. It tells us how far our sample mean might be from the true population mean.

The formula for the margin of error depends on the standard deviation and the sample size. A common formula uses the z score multiplied by the standard error. Remember that the z score relates to the confidence level we choose.

items: Middle: Standard Error ( rac{ ext{SD}}{ ext{sqrt}(n)})

explain.say: Next, we build the interval itself. The confidence interval is simply the sample mean plus or minus the margin of error. This gives us a lower bound and an upper bound for the true mean.

items: Subtract margin of error ( ar{x} - ext{ME})
Add margin of error ( ar{x} + ext{ME})
Result: Lower bound to Upper bound

explain.say: Finally, interpretation is key. If we are 95 percent confident, it means that if we repeated this sampling process many times, ninety-five percent of the resulting intervals would contain the true population mean.

draw.text: 95% CI: 95% chance the true mean is in this range.

faq.q: What does the 95 percent confidence level actually mean?
faq.a: It means that if we repeated the sampling process many times, ninety-five percent of the intervals we calculate would contain the true population mean. It does not mean there is a ninety-five percent chance the true mean is in this specific interval.
asks: What does 95 percent confidence really mean?
Is 95 percent confidence the probability the mean is in the interval?

faq.q: When can I use this method to find an interval?
faq.a: You must know the sample size and have a measure of the population standard deviation or use the sample standard deviation if the sample size is large enough. The data should also be random.
asks: What are the conditions for using CIs?
Do I need a normal distribution for this?

faq.q: Does the margin of error change if I increase my sample size?
faq.a: Yes, the margin of error decreases as the sample size increases. This makes our estimate more precise because we have more information from our sample.
asks: How does sample size affect the error?
If I take more samples, is my estimate better?

faq.q: If I want to be more confident, should I change the margin of error?
faq.a: To be more confident, you must accept a wider margin of error. A higher confidence level means a wider range to capture the true mean.
asks: Can I make the interval smaller and still be confident?
What happens if I choose 99 percent confidence?

faq.q: Is the sample mean always the center of the confidence interval?
faq.a: Yes, the sample mean always serves as the center point for the confidence interval. The margin of error extends equally in both directions from the sample mean.
asks: Is the average always in the middle of the interval?

facts: A confidence interval provides a range estimate for a population parameter.
The margin of error accounts for the uncertainty due to sampling variability.
Larger sample sizes result in smaller margins of error, increasing precision.
The confidence level dictates the z score used in the calculation.

quiz.say: A study finds a sample mean of 50 with a margin of error of 3. What is the lower bound of the interval?
quiz.why: The lower bound is found by subtracting the margin of error from the sample mean, giving 50 minus 3 equals 47.

wrong.0: This incorrectly states the margin of error as the answer, ignoring the sample mean.
wrong.1: This incorrectly assumes the margin of error is zero, providing no range.
wrong.3: This incorrectly adds the margin of error to the mean, which finds the upper bound.

quiz.say: If you increase your sample size, what happens to the margin of error?
quiz.why: Because the sample size is in the denominator of the margin of error formula, increasing it makes the overall value smaller.

wrong.0: This confuses the relationship; more data leads to less uncertainty, not more.
wrong.1: The margin of error is directly related to sample size, so it must change.
wrong.2: The margin of error depends on standard deviation and sample size, not the sample mean itself.
